question: How are user demonstrations represented in domain-specific-language programs and used for automation tasks?

sections.title: Interaction Paradigms and Representation
sections.text: In the DiLogics framework, user demonstrations are captured through a Program-by-Demonstration (PBD) approach that prioritizes direct interaction with target applications over traditional code writing [1]. Rather than requiring users to manually construct syntax, the system allows individuals to initiate a web recording session and physically demonstrate the specific actions required for each step of a task [1]. This process involves recording the mappings between diverse high-level specifications and the corresponding low-level user interface (UI) actions [1]. By capturing these mappings, the system constructs automation programs that possess malleable programming logic, enabling the insertion of appropriate UI actions for each step in real time [1]. This method effectively reduces the level of expertise required from system designers, as the neurosymbolic domain-specific language (DSL) abstracts away complex implementation details [1].

citations.title: dilogics: creating web automation programs with diverse logics

sections.title: Verbal and Demonstrative Input Processing
sections.text: Beyond direct UI interaction, other systems like Pumice utilize a different mechanism for capturing user intent. In this approach, an agent prompts the user to either verbally explain or demonstrate how to fulfill a specific resolve() function [2]. When a verbal explanation is provided, the system parses this input into an expression that matches the original type within the target DSL [2]. For instance, if the user describes a Boolean concept, the system generates a corresponding Boolean expression [2]. This generated expression then replaces the original resolve() function, effectively integrating the user's demonstration into the program's logic [2]. This highlights a distinct representation strategy where natural language or verbal cues are translated into formal DSL constructs, contrasting with the direct UI action mapping seen in DiLogics [1] [2].

sections.title: Automation Logic and Limitations
sections.text: The primary utility of these demonstration-based representations is the construction of automated workflows. In DiLogics, the recorded mappings allow the system to build automation programs that can execute tasks by inserting proper UI actions dynamically [1]. However, this approach has specific constraints regarding the complexity of the logic that can be automated. The system is unable to perform logics that require constant analysis of the website's state [1]. This limitation suggests that while the PBD approach is effective for tasks with relatively static or predictable UI interactions, it may struggle with scenarios where the automation must continuously evaluate and adapt to changing environmental conditions [1]. The neurosymbolic DSL helps mitigate some design complexity [1], but the fundamental reliance on recorded UI actions and mapped specifications defines the boundary of what can be automated without deeper state analysis [1].

question: Have specialized approaches been developed for providing LLM assistance when people author SQL queries?

sections.title: Overview of LLM Adoption in SQL Generation
sections.text: Large language models have attracted significant interest in the domain of SQL generation due to their robust text generation capabilities [1]. While general text-to-SQL systems are common, specialized approaches have emerged to address specific user interaction patterns, particularly those involving real-time assistance during query authoring. These specialized methods differ from standard natural language querying by focusing on the mechanics of how users construct queries, requiring distinct architectural and performance considerations.

sections.title: Autocompletion and Latency Constraints
sections.text: A primary area of specialization is the automation of SQL query completion, often referred to as autocompletion, which assists authors as they type [2]. This task presents unique challenges compared to standard text-to-SQL translation. Specifically, the latency constraints for an autocompletion tool are significantly tighter than those for natural language querying, necessitating faster response times to maintain user flow [2]. To meet these performance requirements, the training data for such models must differ from that of standard text-to-SQL systems; instead of relying on pairs of natural language text and SQL, the LLM must be trained on a large corpus of SQL queries alone [2]. This shift in training data allows the model to predict the next tokens of a SQL statement more effectively in a low-latency environment.

sections.title: Architectural Innovations for Speed
sections.text: To address the stringent latency demands of real-time SQL assistance, specific model architectures have been developed. Consistency Large Language Models (CLLMs) represent one such innovation, featuring an enhanced model architecture designed specifically to reduce latency and accelerate the generation of SQL queries [3]. By optimizing the inference process, CLLMs provide a technical solution to the speed bottlenecks inherent in standard LLM-based generation, making them suitable for interactive tools where immediate feedback is critical.

sections.title: Schema Linking and Retrieval Augmentation
sections.text: Beyond raw generation speed, specialized approaches also focus on improving the accuracy of schema linking, which is crucial for generating valid SQL against complex database structures. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) based text-to-SQL systems integrate dynamic retrieval capabilities with generative models to enhance the quality of SQL query generation [3]. This integration allows the model to access relevant schema information dynamically, reducing hallucinations and improving syntactic correctness. Furthermore, specific algorithms have been developed to optimize this linking process for large-scale databases. SchemagraphSQL utilizes pathfinding graph algorithms to perform efficient schema linking, demonstrating superior performance compared to both fine-tuned and other specialized methods [5][5]. Additionally, techniques for scaling Text2SQL have been introduced that employ LLM-efficient schema filtering using Functional Dependency Graph Rerankers, further refining the selection of relevant database elements prior to generation [4].

question: How can the integration of GIS spatial analysis techniques with economic modeling improve the accuracy and effectiveness of environmental policy ?

sections.title: Methodological Integration of Spatial and Economic Frameworks
sections.text: The convergence of geographic information systems with spatial statistical analysis offers a significantly more sophisticated approach to conducting regional economic analyses [2]. By merging these distinct analytical domains, researchers can move beyond traditional non-spatial methods to capture the complex spatial dependencies inherent in economic data [2]. This integration allows for a more nuanced understanding of how economic variables interact with geographic boundaries and spatial distributions, thereby enhancing the precision of regional assessments [2]. The application of such integrated techniques is not merely theoretical but has been demonstrated in practical applications where the linkage of GIS with both environmental and economic models facilitates a comprehensive evaluation of policy impacts [1]. Specifically, the connection between geographic information systems and dual modeling frameworks enables the assessment of hypothetical scenarios that involve changes in land use [1]. This two-step procedural approach ensures that the spatial dimensions of economic and environmental factors are rigorously examined, providing a robust foundation for policy analysis [1].

sections.title: Application in Environmental Policy Assessment
sections.text: A primary application of this integrated methodology is the evaluation of environmental consequences resulting from policy-driven changes in land use [1]. For instance, the potential impacts of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) Reform have been analyzed by linking GIS with specific environmental and economic models [1]. This approach allows policymakers to simulate and evaluate the environmental outcomes of hypothetical land use changes that are driven by agricultural policy reforms [1]. By utilizing a two-step process that connects geographic data with economic and environmental simulations, the analysis can isolate and quantify the specific effects of policy interventions on the landscape [1]. The integration of these models provides a structured framework for understanding how economic incentives, such as those found in the CAP, translate into physical changes in land use and subsequent environmental impacts [1]. This capability is crucial for designing policies that aim to balance economic objectives with environmental sustainability, as it provides a clear line of causality between policy decisions and their spatial and ecological consequences [1].

Furthermore, the effectiveness of policy evaluation is enhanced by the ability to link GIS with environmental and economic models to assess the consequences of land use changes [1]. The two-step procedure of linking these systems ensures that both the economic drivers and the environmental results are considered in a unified spatial context [1]. question: How can question generation be used to mitigate hallucination in LLMs?

sections.title: Core Mechanism: Retrieval Over Generation
sections.text: The primary strategy for mitigating hallucination in Large Language Models (LLMs) involves shifting from generative answering to direct retrieval of original content. By bypassing the generation step, the system ensures that responses are grounded in existing data, thereby eliminating the risk of fabricating information [1]. This approach is particularly effective in open-domain question answering, where high precision is required to avoid the inaccuracies inherent in generated text [1]. The fundamental argument is that a retrieval mechanism capable of precisely identifying relevant text serves as a practical and useful method for reducing hallucinations, especially in structured knowledge bases like Wikipedia [1].

sections.title: Question-to-Question (Q2Q) Retrieval Framework
sections.text: A specific implementation of this strategy is the Question-to-Question (Q2Q) retrieval approach, introduced in a 2025 paper focused on hallucination-free knowledge access [1]. Conventional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models often suffer from low semantic similarity between natural language questions and document passages due to structural and lexical differences [1]. This 'question-to-passage' comparison typically yields low cosine similarity scores, often in the 0.4-0.7 range, which hinders high-precision retrieval for specific queries [1]. To overcome this, the Q2Q method uses an instruction-tuned LLM to generate a comprehensive set of questions for each logical content unit within the knowledge base, rather than embedding the document content directly [1]. By comparing user queries to these generated questions, the system achieves high cosine similarity, exceeding 0.9 for relevant pairs, which enables highly precise retrieval [1].

sections.text: The Q2Q framework has been demonstrated on Wikipedia and Wikidata, including multimedia content through structured fact retrieval [1]. These technical choices allow the system to maintain high precision while avoiding the generation step that typically introduces hallucinations [1].

sections.title: Question Decomposition and Graph-Based Approaches
sections.text: Beyond direct retrieval, decomposing complex questions into simpler sub-questions based on identified topic entities can guide LLMs to better answer the original query, thereby reducing hallucinations [2]. This decomposition process addresses the relationship between topic entities and potential answers, allowing the model to handle complex queries more accurately [2]. In the context of 'Paths over Graph' approaches, the question analysis phase is divided into two parts and executed within a single LLM call using an example-based prompt to further reduce hallucinations [2]. This structured analysis helps the model navigate knowledge graphs more effectively, ensuring that the final answer is supported by verified paths rather than generated guesses [2].

sections.text: The necessity of these mitigation strategies is highlighted by baseline hallucination rates in LLMs. For instance, InstructGPT models make up information not present in the input about half as often as GPT-3, with hallucination rates of 21% compared to 41% for GPT-3 [5] [3]. Additionally, longer captions tend to have higher hallucination rates, indicating that output length is a risk factor [5] [3]. In specialized domains, such as scientific publication search, leveraging LLMs to retrieve specific and general publications while addressing content hallucination challenges is a key use case [4]. The Q2Q approach, by ensuring responses are retrieved rather than generated, offers a robust solution for these high-stakes applications where factual accuracy is paramount [1] [4].

sections.title: System Architecture and Workflow
sections.text: The Ontology-based and User-focused Automatic Text Summarization (OATS) system integrates cognitive and computational methods through a two-module design [1]. The first module performs ontology-based topic identification to filter documents relevant to specific user interests, while the second module generates user-focused summaries [1]. This pipeline is motivated by the spirit of the Clinical Quality Measure (CQM) ontology, adapted here to identify COVID-19 risk factors from unstructured articles [1]. The system utilizes an ontology-based approach that employs concept graphs to represent knowledge derived from unstructured text, combined with a matching algorithm [1]. A key advantage of this architecture is its ability to extract summary sentences from unstructured text without relying on manually annotated knowledge, distinguishing it from other ontology-based automatic text summarization systems [1].

sections.title: User-Centric Customization and Question-Answering
sections.text: The summarization module is highly customizable, requiring users to define specific questions based on their interests and determine the order of these questions, which dictates the order of sentences in the generated summary [1]. The system utilizes a question-answering model to extract answers from user-specified questions [1]. The QA model demonstrates the ability to distinguish between highly similar numerical details, such as the number of patients enrolled versus the number screened [1]. For methodology-related questions (Q1 through Q6), the extracted answers achieved over 50% accuracy [1]. However, the QA approach has limitations; it requires a standardized set of questions to access information that may be presented in non-standardized ways across different documents, such as risk from hypertension [1]. Additionally, the performance of the QA model can be limited by the inaccessibility of text sections that contain the optimal answers [1].

sections.title: Performance Evaluation and Risk Factor Analysis
sections.text: The system was evaluated on four specific COVID-19 risk factors, generally achieving high precision and acceptable recall scores [1]. For Hypertension, the system achieved a precision of 0.93 and a recall of 0.84 [1]. For Diabetes, the precision was 0.92 with a recall of 0.76 [1]. Obesity yielded the highest precision at 1.0, with a recall of 0.71 [1]. COPD showed slightly poorer performance compared to the other factors, with a precision of 0.81 and a recall of 0.60 [1]. The handling of the COPD acronym presents specific challenges; using only 'COPD' and its full name 'chronic obstructive pulmonary disease' results in low recall, while separating the acronym into four words and measuring distance from each word leads to low precision because the term 'chronic' is commonplace [1]. To address this, potential improvements include adding an algorithm to extract an acronym's corresponding full name or performing task-specific training to enhance the word2vec model [1].
